modules.summary: Self-similarity in nature and art, then three mathematical fractals built by repeating one rule: the Sierpinski carpet, the Sierpinski gasket, and the Koch snowflake, each showing how counts, holes, area and perimeter grow or shrink.

media.title: Self-similar shapes
labels: the same rule at every scale
media.context: A shape is self-similar when it is built from smaller copies of itself, one rule applied again and again at smaller scales. The worked example asks whether a fern, whose leaflets each look like a smaller whole fern, is self-similar. The figure zooms in twice and finds the same shape.
media.description: Self-similar shapes: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'A fern frond is made of leaflets, and each leaflet looks like a smaller whole fern. Is the fern self-similar?'.

source_image.caption: Self-similar shapes: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'A fern frond is made of leaflets, and each leaflet looks like a smaller whole fern. Is the fern self-similar?'.

media.teaching_notes: Zoom in twice and ask what has changed about the shape; the answer is only the size. Ask what rule is being repeated. Then ask whether a circle is self-similar and why the answer is no.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a magnified part that does not resemble the whole; a zoom sequence that changes the shape; a photorealistic botanical illustration; a claim of self-similarity for a shape that is not; more than three zoom levels crowding the figure
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A fern frond is drawn flat at the left, built from leaflets along a central stem. A magnifier circle picks out one leaflet and enlarges it beside the frond, showing it to have the same branching shape as the whole. A second magnifier picks out one part of that leaflet and enlarges it again, showing the same shape a third time, with the three drawings joined by zoom arrows and a tag reading the same rule at every scale. A verdict card reads self-similar, ticked. To the side, two further self-similar examples are sketched small, a branching tree and a lightning fork, with a note that one rule repeated at smaller scales builds all of them. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: a fern frond; one leaflet; one part of that leaflet; the same shape again; the same rule at every scale; self-similar; a tree; a lightning fork.
media.accuracy_constraints:
Each magnified part must be drawn with the same branching shape as the whole frond.
The zoom sequence must run through at least three scales.
The verdict must be that the fern is self-similar.
The further examples must genuinely be self-similar shapes.
The drawing must stay flat and diagrammatic, not photorealistic.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Self Similarity Zoomer
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Part 2, chapter 4 'Exploring Some Geometric Themes', the fractals half. It opens the fractal thread: self similarity has to be CHECKABLE before any counting rule later in the chapter means anything, so the tool is read before the removal counts, the perimeter multiplier or the replacement rule. NCERT's vocabulary is STEP (Step 0 is the untouched seed), not depth, iteration or recursion; the tool labels its read-out 'Step (depth)' once and 'Step' after, and carries the bank's own wording of 'depth' verbatim inside the questions. No limits, no geometric series and no fractal dimension: those are not Class 8.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's choice, the correct one, and the matched structures.
whatYouLearned: A self similar figure is built from smaller copies of itself, so a part that carries structure magnifies into the whole figure again
The repetition is exact, because the magnified view is regenerated from the rule and never enlarged from a picture
The drawing has to stop somewhere and the rule does not, so a finite picture can record an endless repetition

overview.goal: The student identifies the repeating sub structure in a fractal, predicts what a zoom will reveal, and says whether the repetition ever stops.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying two panels, the whole figure on one and the magnified contents of a small window on the other, the way a map and its inset are printed on a single sheet. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class splits over whether the corner of the figure is merely a bit like the whole or exactly the whole again, and the zoom window is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A self similar figure is built from smaller copies of itself, so magnifying any part reveals the same structure again. The repetition is exact rather than a resemblance, and it does not stop: the rule can be applied at any scale, even though the drawing has to stop somewhere.
overview.purpose: The student identifies the repeating sub structure in a fractal, predicts what a zoom will reveal, and says whether the repetition ever stops.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Whole left and magnification right on a wide frame, stacked on a 390 px frame with the connecting line running vertically. The window handle keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not draw the magnification while a prediction is still open, and never scale a bitmap to produce it. A pixellated zoom would teach that self similarity degrades with scale.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Each stage of the construction replaces every piece with a scaled copy of the whole arrangement, so any piece at any stage is a scaled copy of the figure. Magnifying that piece therefore reproduces the figure exactly. The drawing stops when the pieces become too small to render, but the rule that generates them has no such limit, which is the distinction the tool has to be honest about. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.summary: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the fractal and the zoom region from its own data, shows the question, then reveals the magnification, the matched sub structure and the answer together as one beat. learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): Self similarity says every part that carries structure repeats the whole, not that every region carries structure. Breaks: Reading self similarity as a promise that any window at all will reveal more detail. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): The rendering depth belongs to the drawing; the rule that generates the figure has no last stage. Breaks: The drawn figure mistaken for the mathematical object, so the repetition is thought to stop where the picture does. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): A zoom is a regeneration at a finer scale, so the drawing has to be extended rather than stretched. Breaks: Believing the detail was already sitting in the picture and only needed enlarging. ML4 (Hard, Conceptual): Self similarity is an exact match of structure, so almost right is wrong. Breaks: Self similarity read as approximate resemblance rather than exact repetition. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): The rule, not the picture, is the source of detail at every scale. Breaks: Treating the rendered image as the object, so a zoom is imagined as a stretch of what is already drawn.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the fractal and a zoom window placed on a corner, with the magnified view HIDDEN, and asks the class to choose the thumbnail showing what the zoom will reveal. Beat 2 zooms and the matching sub structure lights in both the whole and the magnification, joined by a line. Beat 3 zooms a second level and the pattern repeats again, then asks whether it ever stops. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with moveWindow, zoomIn, highlightMatch and say. No drag: the agent moves the window by named region.
whatYouLearned: A self similar figure is built from smaller copies of itself, so a part that carries structure magnifies into the whole figure again
The repetition is exact, because the magnified view is regenerated from the rule and never enlarged from a picture
The drawing has to stop somewhere and the rule does not, so a finite picture can record an endless repetition
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the whole figure with the zoom window resting on one corner and the magnified panel empty, and ask the class to say out loud which of the thumbnails the zoom will show. Commit the class choice on the prediction pad. Targets the window on the top corner at zoom level 0. Never magnify before the prediction is committed, and never say what the panel will hold at this call. Call 2. Magnify one level and let the matching sub structure light in both panels with the connecting line drawn between them. Point at the whole figure and then at the magnified panel. Targets zoom level 1 with the same window. Read the zoom level and the rendering depth from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Magnify a second level so the same structure appears again, then ask the class whether the repetition ever stops. Targets zoom level 2 and the depth readout. Say plainly that the drawing stops and the rule does not, and read the depth and any extension notice from getState().truth.

hunts: EMPTY WINDOW HUNT: find a window whose magnification shows nothing, and say what the rule did to that region.
EXACT MATCH HUNT: find a part that matches the whole exactly, then find one that is only close, and say which is a real part.
DEPTH CHASE: zoom until the tool has to extend the drawing, and say what changed and what did not.
SCALE LADDER: pick a depth, predict the magnification that restores it to full width, then check the readout.

whatYouLearned: A self similar figure is built from smaller copies of itself, so a part that carries structure magnifies into the whole figure again
The repetition is exact, because the magnified view is regenerated from the rule and never enlarged from a picture
The drawing has to stop somewhere and the rule does not, so a finite picture can record an endless repetition

observationsAndConclusions.why: The tool regenerates the figure from its rule at the new scale instead of enlarging the pixels it had already drawn
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The magnified corner resolves into the whole figure again, not into a blurred patch
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Exact self similarity means the rule can be run at any scale, so magnifying reveals structure rather than destroying it

observationsAndConclusions.why: The rule leaves that region empty at every later stage, so there is no structure inside it to reveal
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A window dropped on a hole magnifies to nothing at all
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Self similarity promises that every part carrying structure repeats the whole, never that every region carries structure

observationsAndConclusions.why: The drawn figure was only generated to a finite depth, and more depth has to be produced before the magnified panel can be honest
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Zooming far enough makes the tool announce that it has extended the drawing
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The picture is a finite record of an infinite rule, so where the drawing stops says nothing about where the repetition stops

media.description: Two panels stand side by side on a plain working ground, the whole figure on the left with a square zoom window outlined on it, and the contents of that window magnified on the right, the way a map and its inset are printed on one sheet. A dashed cone joins the window to the magnified panel and carries the magnification as a plate, so the two views can never be read apart. The magnified panel is REGENERATED from the figure's own rule at the finer scale and never enlarged from what was already drawn: the window's side is exactly one part in factor-to-the-power-zoom of the whole, so the drawn magnification IS the reported one by construction. Each of the three figures carries its own pair of numbers - the triangle removal figure magnifies by 2 a step and puts 3 copies in place of each piece, the square removal figure by 3 with 8 copies, the bumped outline by 3 with 4 - and every read-out is taken from the figure actually drawn rather than from a constant. Recursion stops when a piece gets too small to mark, and the step it reached is REPORTED, so the drawing's own limit is visible while the rule's absence of one is stated beside it. A window dropped on a hole magnifies to a genuinely empty panel, because the generator finds nothing there to make.

concept.notation: A sub structure is a part of the figure that matches the whole exactly, not approximately. A zoom level is one magnification step of the generating rule.
concept.statement: A self similar figure is built from smaller copies of itself, so magnifying any part reveals the same structure again. The repetition is exact rather than a resemblance, and it does not stop: the rule can be applied at any scale, even though the drawing has to stop somewhere.
prerequisites: scaling a figure by a factor
misconceptions: Self similarity read as approximate resemblance rather than exact repetition.
The drawn figure mistaken for the mathematical object, so the repetition is thought to stop where the picture does.
concept.why_it_is_true: Each stage of the construction replaces every piece with a scaled copy of the whole arrangement, so any piece at any stage is a scaled copy of the figure. Magnifying that piece therefore reproduces the figure exactly. The drawing stops when the pieces become too small to render, but the rule that generates them has no such limit, which is the distinction the tool has to be honest about.
worked_numbers: A corner of the triangle removal figure at one zoom level is that whole figure again.
At two levels it is that whole figure a third time.
The drawing stops at the rendering depth; the rule does not.

answer_key.worked: Zooming into any sub triangle of the triangle removal figure shows that whole figure again, exactly, at every level.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 settles the argument the class is actually having - is the corner merely LIKE the whole figure, or IS it the whole figure. The magnified panel is generated from the rule rather than enlarged, so the answer is a picture and not a claim: the corner resolves into the same figure with the same branches, and the matched sub copy lights in both panels at once with the cone drawn between them.

Beat 2 exists for the single hardest sub skill on this topic: telling the COUNT from the FACTOR. One step of the triangle rule puts 3 copies in place of each piece, and those three are outlined and numbered on the figure itself - while the plate on the cone reads ×2, because each copy is half the side. A class that says 'three copies, so magnify by three' is looking at both numbers side by side and can see they are different numbers.

Beat 3 carries the idea to its useful edge. Zooming three levels forces the drawing to be regenerated from Step 4 to Step 7 and the strip says so out loud. Say plainly that what changed was the PICTURE: the rule already described that level, and it describes the next one too. Read the step and the extension notice off the screen, never from memory.

media.title: The Coastline That Has No Length
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening on scale and on what a single picture can say, and withholds every result: no count is given, no perimeter is computed and no relationship between views is stated.
media.description: A coastline seems to have no settled length: measure it with a long ruler and you get one answer, switch to a shorter ruler and the answer gets bigger, and keep shortening the ruler and the number continues to climb. A triangle can behave just as strangely, growing smaller triangles along every edge while its border becomes longer at each step even though the whole figure remains inside a small patch of the page. Then a fern offers a completely different kind of surprise: one leaflet looks like the whole fern at a smaller scale, and a piece of that leaflet repeats the same pattern again. Coastlines, lightning bolts and tall temple towers show similar tiny copies of themselves, while a folded box reminds us that a single object can also look completely different from different viewpoints. Together, these examples raise questions about length, scale, self-similarity and what a picture can really tell us about a shape.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse curiosity about shapes that change with scale and about what a single view can determine. Key teaching points: 1) A coastline measurement depends on the ruler used. 2) A repeating construction can lengthen a border indefinitely. 3) A solid can present very different outlines from different sides. 4) One picture is rarely enough to identify a solid. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume any length has one correct value. 2) Students often identify a solid from a single view. Pause points: 0:32, at the end of bumps on every edge: ask why a shorter ruler gives a longer coastline. 1:16, just before the opening question: ask what solid could give all three of those outlines. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask how they would measure a coastline. After viewing, ask how many views a solid needs.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
Bring together the chapter's two striking ideas: measurements that refuse to settle and shapes that repeat themselves at smaller scales. Begin with a coastline and a growing triangle to show how increasingly fine measurement can keep changing a boundary length. Then introduce the fern and other natural forms to show the opposite surprise: the same shape can appear again and again at different scales. Use a folded box as a contrasting example of how a single object can present different shapes from different views. Do not explain the mathematical rule yet. The film should open questions about length, scale, self-similarity and shape.

STORY

A coastline is measured with a long ruler and produces one answer. A shorter ruler gives a larger answer, and as the ruler becomes shorter the number keeps climbing without settling.

A triangle then grows small triangles on every edge, repeating the construction again and again. Its border becomes longer at every step while the whole figure remains inside a small patch of the page.

A folded sheet of card becomes a box, and the same box appears as three completely different shapes when viewed from three different sides.

Then a fern is examined at three scales. One leaflet held beside the whole fern resembles the same fern at a smaller scale. A piece snipped from that leaflet repeats the pattern again.

The same visual idea appears in coastlines, lightning bolts and tall temple towers, where smaller structures resemble the larger structure.

The film should leave the student wondering how a boundary can keep gaining length, how a shape can contain smaller copies of itself, and why ordinary smooth shapes such as a ball do not behave in the same way.

RENDERER

Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

ASSETS

No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace, NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL

COASTLINE

The coastline is measured with a long ruler and then a shorter ruler.
The shorter ruler gives a bigger answer.
As the ruler shortens, the number keeps climbing.
There is no sign of the measurement settling.

TRIANGLE

A triangle grows small triangles on every edge.
The process repeats again and again.
The border gets longer at every step.
The whole figure remains inside a small patch of the page.

BOX

The same box looks like three completely different shapes from three sides.

FERN

OTHER EXAMPLES

Coastlines.
Lightning bolts.
Tall temple towers.

CONTRAST

A smooth ball does not display the same self-similar behaviour.

CENTRAL QUESTIONS

Can a boundary have no settled length?
How can the same shape appear at several scales?
Why can a picture look different depending on the viewpoint?
What rule could build a shape out of smaller versions of itself?

WITHHELD

The mathematical definition.
The formula.
The construction rule.
Any explanation of why the coastline measurement keeps increasing.
Any explanation of why the fern repeats its form.
Any formal terminology for the phenomenon.
Any solution or conclusion beyond the observations.

topics.summary: A shape is self-similar when smaller copies of the whole appear inside it, made by one rule repeated at smaller and smaller scales. The learner tells a self-similar shape from a plain one and names the repeating rule.

content.text: A shape is self-similar when it is built from smaller copies of the whole shape. One rule is applied again and again at smaller and smaller scales. A fern is self-similar because each leaflet is a smaller fern, and each part of that leaflet is a smaller fern again. A tree, a coastline, a lightning bolt and a tall temple tower are self-similar in the same way. A plain smooth shape, like a ball or a straight line, is not self-similar, because zooming in shows no smaller copy of the whole and no new repeating detail. When each step of the rule makes a fixed number of copies, the total number of copies grows by multiplying by that number every step.

segments.summary: Self-similarity in nature and art, then three mathematical fractals built by repeating one rule: the Sierpinski carpet, the Sierpinski gasket, and the Koch snowflake, each showing how counts, holes, area and perimeter grow or shrink.

media.description: A 100-second whiteboard-style animation. Seconds 0 to 30 show Step 0 to Step 2 of the carpet, with on-screen tags tracking the counts 1, 8, 64 as each step plays. Seconds 30 to 70 derive R_{n+1} = 8 R_n by highlighting how each shaded square becomes 8 smaller shaded squares, then unroll the recursion to R_n = 8 to the n. WHAT TO PAUSE AT: Pause at 28s and ask `What operation takes R_1 = 8 to R_2 = 64 - adding 8 or multiplying by 8?` - accept either guess, then play and compare. Pause at 55s (attempt-before-reveal for the holes) and ask `Now how would you count the holes at the next step?` - this is the critical attempt-before-reveal moment for the H recursion. WHAT TO ASK AFTER: Ask `Why does multiplying by 8 produce a much faster growth than adding 8?` to stress the ERROR ALERT that mistakes R_n for the sequence 1, 9, 17, 25.

media.teaching_notes: WHEN: Play at the start of the topic, just after the HOOK about ferns and the temple has been read aloud, to anchor the new word `fractal` in familiar images before any formal definition. WHAT TO PAUSE AT: Pause at 50s (end of the temple scene) and ask `What other shapes from your surroundings repeat this way?` - this is the attempt-before-reveal moment before the Sierpinski Carpet construction begins. Pause again at 75s (after Step 1 is shown) and ask `What would you do next to produce Step 2?` - let students predict that the same rule repeats on each of the 8 remaining squares. WHAT TO ASK AFTER: After the video, ask `Why does the fern count as a fractal while a printed bedsheet with the same flower pattern does not?` to stress that `copies inside copies` is the defining rule.

topics.summary: Cutting a square into 9 and removing the centre, over and over, multiplies the remaining squares by 8 each step while holes pile up and the leftover area shrinks toward zero. The learner counts survivors, removals, holes and area.

content.text: In the Sierpinski carpet you cut a square into 9 equal squares and remove the middle one, leaving 8. Then you do the same to each of those 8, and so on. Because every surviving square makes 8 new survivors, the number of remaining squares is multiplied by 8 at each step. So after 1 step there are 8, after 2 steps 8 x 8 = 64, after 3 steps 512, and after n steps the count is 8 multiplied by itself n times. The squares removed at a step are the centres punched out, one per square, so the number removed at a step is exactly the number that remained the step before.

concepts.concept_name: Counting the squares that remain

source_ai_reasoning.note: Posed and explained by the AI in the AI section, separate from the tool-answered practice. Each carries a full step-by-step explanation of the reasoning behind the answer.

content.text: Every time a square is cut, its centre becomes a hole, and holes never fill back in. So the holes add up: 1 after step 1, then 1 + 8 = 9, then 1 + 8 + 64 = 73, and so on, adding the previous number of squares each time. At the same time, cutting a square into 9 and keeping 8 leaves 8/9 of its area. So the leftover area is multiplied by 8/9 every step: 8/9, then 64/81, then 512/729. Because 8/9 is less than 1, the leftover area heads toward zero, even though the number of remaining squares keeps growing by 8 each step.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why the Sierpinski carpet keeps more squares than it removes, and determine that cutting each square into 9 and dropping the centre leaves 8 survivors, so the count multiplies by 8 each step and equals 8 raised to the step number. They will explain that the squares removed at a step match the number that remained the step before.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Fractals: shapes that repeat at every scale
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why the carpet fills with holes yet still holds squares, and determine that every surviving square opens one new hole while old holes stay, so the total is a running sum of 1 plus 8 plus 64 and onward. They will explain that keeping 8 of 9 parts multiplies the leftover area by 8/9 each step, so the area shrinks toward zero even as the squares grow.

media.accuracy_constraints:
The midpoints must be marked at the exact centre of each side.
Joining them must make four equal equilateral triangles, each with sides half the original.
Only the middle triangle may be removed, leaving exactly 3 survivors.
The counts must run 1, 3, 9 and 27 for steps 0 to 3.
Every step must multiply the count by 3.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Part 2, 'Exploring Some Geometric Themes' - the Fractals section, where the Sierpinski gasket is built by repeated middle-triangle removal and the class tabulates triangles remaining, holes and area step by step. This is the FIRST counting rule of the chapter: multiplicative growth has to be established here or the perimeter argument two topics later cannot surprise anyone. overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground holding one filled triangle that is losing middle triangles stage by stage, with a stage slider and two readouts beneath it and a magnifier panel to the side. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class reads the counts three and nine and calls the next one twelve, and the third stage is asked to be drawn and counted.
overview.concept: At each stage the middle triangle is removed from every remaining triangle, so each triangle becomes three. The count is therefore multiplied by three every stage, giving three to the power n, and the remaining area is multiplied by three quarters. Growth by multiplication is what makes the counts climb so fast.
overview.purpose: The student applies an iteration rule repeatedly, predicts the count of pieces at a later stage, and states the rule for stage n.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with the stage slider and count readout beneath. The zoom panel opens to the side on a wide frame and below on a 390 px frame. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the count while a prediction is still open, and never draw beyond the stated cap. Drawing past the cap would produce a figure too dense to count honestly.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Every remaining triangle is treated identically, so whatever happens to one happens to all. One triangle becomes three, so the whole count is multiplied by three. Since each of the three has a quarter of the parent's area, three quarters of the area survives each stage, which is why the area shrinks while the count grows. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): Stage 0 is the state the rule counts from, so the count starts at 1 rather than at 3. Breaks: Treating the first drawn removal as stage 0, which shifts every later count by one. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): Applying the rule to every triangle multiplies the count, so the counts climb as powers. Breaks: Iteration counts assumed to grow by addition, so a later stage is predicted far too low. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): The count comes from the rule, so it is available at stages the drawing refuses. Breaks: Believing a count can only be known for a stage that has been drawn. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): A rule that fits one stage is not a rule; it has to be tested at a stage it was not fitted to. Breaks: Accepting a formula because it matches the first case that was checked. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): More pieces does not mean more area: the count multiplies by three while the area is multiplied by three quarters. Breaks: Assuming a figure made of more pieces must cover more of the plane.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open at stage 2 with the counts for stages 1 and 2 listed, stage 3 undrawn and no count for it, and ask the class to say out loud how many triangles stage 3 will hold. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Targets stage 2 with the count table on. Never advance before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Advance one stage so every remaining triangle loses its middle at the same moment, and let the count land beside the committed guess. Point at the count readout and then at the remaining area fraction. Targets stage 3. Read the count and the area fraction from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Ask for the count at a stage far beyond anything that can be drawn, and let the rule produce it with no picture. Targets a far stage count at stage 10 with the count table on. Name why the drawing stops and the rule does not, and read the count from getState().truth.

hunts: PREDICT THEN RUN: predict the count two stages ahead, then advance and measure how far an added guess falls short.
AREA AGAINST COUNT: find the stage where the count first passes 100 and say what the area has done by then.
ZOOM MATCH: magnify a sub triangle and say what would have to differ for the match to be only a resemblance.
RULE BREAKER: invent a formula for stage n, then hunt for the first stage it disagrees with.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Every triangle present is replaced by three, so the whole count is multiplied by three at each stage instead of gaining a fixed three
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: An iteration rule compounds, so a sequence that starts slowly overtakes any sequence that climbs by a fixed step

observationsAndConclusions.why: The count is multiplied by three each stage and the area by three quarters, and one factor is above one while the other is below it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The number of pieces climbs while the shaded area falls
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Two quantities driven by the same rule can move in opposite directions, because what matters is the factor each one is multiplied by

observationsAndConclusions.why: The pieces would be smaller than a pixel, so a drawing at that stage would show a dark blur instead of triangles that could be counted
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A stage past the cap is reported as a count with no picture drawn
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A rule outlives the picture that introduced it, which is exactly what makes it worth having

media.description: One filled equilateral triangle stands on a plain working ground, losing its middle triangle at every step. The cut is the three midpoint segments, so each triangle becomes three corner triangles and a point-down hole that is never filled again; the whole set is removed from every remaining triangle at the SAME moment, which is what makes the growth read as multiplication rather than addition. Beside the figure a bar of exactly one square unit empties to three quarters, then nine sixteenths, then twenty-seven sixty-fourths, with a dashed half tick drawn across it so the wrong 1, 3/4, 1/2, 1/4 reading fails on sight while the count climbs 1, 3, 9, 27. A count table lists NCERT's own three columns - solid triangles left, HOLES, and the area as an exact fraction - and when a class has committed a count out loud the teacher's number is ringed BESIDE the true one in the row it was said about, never in place of it. A zoom inset magnifies any sub-triangle and lands it exactly on the figure one step earlier, while the centre hole magnifies to an empty frame. A typed rule is evaluated at four steps and the first disagreeing step is named, so 4n-1 is caught at Step 0, where it asks for -1 triangles, and an off-by-one is caught at Step 0 too. Drawing stops at Step 6 with the reason stated - 729 triangles is the limit of an honest picture - and the count for a step past it is still produced, which is the moment the rule stops describing a drawing and starts being useful.

concept.notation: The count at stage n is written as a power of three. The remaining area is an exact fraction with powers of three and four.
concept.statement: At each stage the middle triangle is removed from every remaining triangle, so each triangle becomes three. The count is therefore multiplied by three every stage, giving three to the power n, and the remaining area is multiplied by three quarters. Growth by multiplication is what makes the counts climb so fast.
misconceptions: Iteration counts assumed to grow by addition, so stage 3 is predicted as 12 rather than 27.
Self similarity treated as a resemblance rather than an exact repetition.
concept.why_it_is_true: Every remaining triangle is treated identically, so whatever happens to one happens to all. One triangle becomes three, so the whole count is multiplied by three. Since each of the three has a quarter of the parent's area, three quarters of the area survives each stage, which is why the area shrinks while the count grows.
worked_numbers: Stage 1 has 3 triangles, stage 2 has 9, stage 3 has 27.
Stage 10 has 3 to the power 10, which is 59049.
The remaining area at stage n is three quarters to the power n.

extra: One cell dividing into three, with every daughter cell dividing again
A branch that splits into three branches, each of which splits into three
A tray of buns cut into three, then every piece cut into three again
A team of three that each recruit three more, followed through the rounds
A folder tree where every folder holds three folders
A savings amount tripled once a year for several years
A drawing whose every line is redrawn as three shorter lines, again and again

The square version of the same idea, where the middle square is removed from every remaining square

answer_key.worked: Each stage multiplies the triangle count by three, so stage n has three to the power n triangles.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn stage: the triangle count, the remaining area as an exact fraction, and whether a typed rule agrees at three stages.
answer_key.precision: Areas are exact fractions with powers of three and four. Counts are exact integers, never estimated from the rendered elements.
answer_key.ground_truth: count(n) = 3 to the power n. remainingArea(n) = three quarters to the power n, as an exact fraction. ruleAgrees(text) = the typed rule evaluated at three stages against count(n).

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

a prediction_made event listed in events[]

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.

steps: Every triangle present becomes 3 smaller triangles, so the count is multiplied by 3.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the count while a prediction is still open, and never draw beyond the stated cap. Drawing past the cap would produce a figure too dense to count honestly.
visual_behaviour.scene: A filled equilateral triangle with removed middle triangles left as holes. Remaining triangles carry the primary accent; the most recently removed ones are outlined so the last step is visible. A zoom panel shows any magnified sub triangle.
visual_behaviour.layout: Figure fills the main panel with the stage slider and count readout beneath. The zoom panel opens to the side on a wide frame and below on a 390 px frame.
readouts: The stage and the triangle count, live once predicted
The remaining area as an exact fraction
The rendering mode and the cap, when they apply
animations: Stage advance: the middle triangles are removed from every remaining triangle at once, so the rule is seen applying uniformly rather than piece by piece.
Count tick: the count multiplies rather than increments, which is drawn as a jump in the readout.
Zoom match: the magnified sub triangle resolves into the same figure, so exactness is watched.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Triangle size is derived from the panel and the stage; above stage 4 rendering moves to canvas and the cap at stage 6 prevents any figure too dense to read.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The removal has to be watched happening to every remaining triangle at once before three to the power n is written, or the stage number is read as something to add and the far stage question has nothing to stand on

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to put the rule and a countable figure on the same screen. Step 2 is the last step a child can count by eye, so the class can check nine solid triangles against the rule before anything larger is drawn. Ask for the Step 3 count OUT LOUD and commit it with predict(); the guess is then ringed beside the true 27 in the table rather than replaced by it, which is the whole of the additive-versus-multiplicative argument.

Beat 2 is the mechanism, not a restatement. Every triangle present becomes three at the same instant, and each of the three carries a quarter of its parent's area - so the count is multiplied by 3 while the area is multiplied by 3/4. The two readouts move in opposite directions in one animation, which is the only honest answer to 'more pieces must mean more area'.

Beat 3 carries the rule past the picture. Step 6 is drawn with the cap and its reason on screen; Step 10 is answered with 59,049 and no figure at all. Read that number from getState().truth or the farStageCount readout, never from your own arithmetic, and name why the drawing stops and the rule does not.
media.generation_prompt: Triangle Removal Iterator: a filled triangle with a stage slider that removes the middle triangle from every remaining one, counting the survivors at each stage
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the stage and the triangle count as the figure stands. 2. Predict the count at the next stage before advancing. 3. Advance the stage and watch every remaining triangle lose its middle at once. 4. Compare your prediction with the count that lands. 5. Open the count table and say what is happening from one row to the next. 6. Zoom into one remaining sub triangle and say what it turns out to be. 7. Type a rule for the count at stage n and test it at three stages. 8. Ask for a stage too far to draw and read the count the rule gives. 9. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: The Triangle That Empties Out
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the Sierpinski gasket. Students know the carpet. The film must not give the counts beyond the first step and must not say where the area is heading.
media.description: Join the midpoints of an equilateral triangle and four smaller triangles appear, all the same size. Remove the middle one and three are left, and repeating on every survivor spreads a lacy pattern of holes across the shape.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Count the triangles at each stage of the Sierpinski gasket and track the shaded area. Key teaching points: 1) Joining the midpoints gives four congruent triangles. 2) Removing the middle leaves three of them. 3) So the count multiplies by three each round. 4) The shaded area shrinks by a quarter each round. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often think more pieces must mean more area. 2) Students often forget that all four sub triangles are congruent. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of a lacy pattern: ask how many triangles remain after two rounds. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what fraction of the area is removed each time. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what joining the midpoints produces. After viewing, ask where the coloured area is heading.

topics.summary: Splitting a triangle at its midpoints into 4 equal triangles and removing the middle, over and over, multiplies the survivors by 3 each step while the area is scaled by 3/4 toward zero. The learner counts triangles, holes and area.

content.text: In the Sierpinski gasket you join the midpoints of an equilateral triangle. This makes 4 smaller triangles that are all the same size and shape, all equilateral, each with sides half as long as the original. Remove the middle one and 3 survive. Doing this to every triangle multiplies the count by 3 each step, so there are 3, then 9, then 27, and after n steps 3 multiplied by itself n times. Since each survivor keeps 3 of its 4 equal parts, the leftover area is multiplied by 3/4 each step, giving 3/4, then 9/16, then 27/64. Because 3/4 is below 1, the area heads toward zero while the number of triangles keeps growing.

labels: raise a triangle on the middle part
media.context: In the Koch snowflake every side is replaced by a bump of four equal segments, so the side count multiplies by four. The worked example starts from a triangle with 3 sides and asks how many sides there are after one step. The figure builds one bump and counts.

Scene: A single straight side is drawn at the top and worked in three stages: divided into three equal parts; a small equilateral triangle raised on the middle part; and the middle part removed, leaving a bump made of four equal segments, each numbered 1 to 4, with a tag reading one side becomes four. Below, the whole snowflake is shown at step 0 as an equilateral triangle with 3 sides, and at step 1 with every side replaced by a bump, with the sides counted as 12 and a strip reading '3 x 4 = 12'. A sequence strip lists 3, 12, 48 and 192 for steps 0 to 3, joined by times 4 arrows. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: divide into three equal parts; raise a triangle on the middle part; drop the middle part; 1; 2; 3; 4; one side becomes four; step 0: 3 sides; 3 x 4 = 12; 3, 12, 48, 192.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The side must be divided into three equal parts, with the bump raised on the middle one.
The finished bump must consist of exactly four equal segments.
The middle part must be removed, not left in place.
The side counts must run 3, 12, 48 and 192 for steps 0 to 3.
Every step must multiply the side count by 4.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: The perimeter that grows forever
labels: each side length becomes one third
the perimeter is multiplied by 4 over 3 each step
a factor above 1 means it grows without limit
media.context: The perimeter is the number of sides times the side length, and each step multiplies the count by four while dividing the length by three. The worked example asks by what factor the perimeter is multiplied. The figure combines the two changes.
media.description: The perimeter that grows forever: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'At each Koch step the sides are multiplied by 4 and each side length becomes one third. By what factor is the perimeter multiplied?'.

source_image.caption: The perimeter that grows forever: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'At each Koch step the sides are multiplied by 4 and each side length becomes one third. By what factor is the perimeter multiplied?'.

media.teaching_notes: Ask whether the perimeter grows or shrinks before computing, since the two changes pull opposite ways. Multiplying them settles it. That the area stays bounded is the surprise worth ending on.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a combined factor other than 4 over 3; the two changes added rather than multiplied; a growth track whose bars shrink; a claim that the area also grows without limit; a factor below 1 described as growing
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: Two change strips run across the top, one reading that the number of sides is multiplied by 4 and one reading that each side length becomes one third. A combining box beneath multiplies them, reading '4 x one third = 4 over 3', with a result card reading the perimeter is multiplied by 4 over 3 at every step. A growth track below shows the perimeter at successive steps as a rising bar chart, each bar 4 over 3 times the one before, with a tag reading that a factor above 1 means the perimeter grows without limit. A contrast note reads that the area stays bounded even though the perimeter does not, drawn as a snowflake outline inside a fixed circle. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: the sides are multiplied by 4; each side length becomes one third; 4 x one third = 4 over 3; the perimeter is multiplied by 4 over 3 each step; a factor above 1 means it grows without limit; the area stays bounded.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The combined factor must be 4 over 3, from 4 times one third.
The two changes must be multiplied, not added.
The growth track bars must each be 4 over 3 times the one before.
The figure must state that the perimeter grows without limit while the area stays bounded.
The factor must be identified as greater than 1.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Bumped Outline Perimeter Iterator
media.context: CBSE Class 8, new NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2, chapter 4 'Exploring Some Geometric Themes', the fractals section - the Koch snowflake. The class has met powers, fractions and perimeter and has NOT met limits, so no limit vocabulary reaches the glass: the screen says 'grows past any number you can name' and 'settles at', never 'unbounded' or 'converges'. It follows the tool that established multiplicative growth, and it is the strongest infinity argument available at this level.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the bounding circle that frames it.

overview.goal: The student computes how the perimeter changes each stage and argues about what happens after many stages, reconciling unbounded perimeter with a bounded region.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground holding one closed outline growing bumps inside a circle that was drawn at the outset and never moves, with the perimeter and its multiplier read out alongside. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class holds that a figure trapped inside a circle must have a boundary of limited length, and the circle is left on screen while the stages run to test it.
overview.concept: Each stage replaces every segment's middle third with two sides of a bump, so three segments become four while each is a third as long. The perimeter is therefore multiplied by four thirds every stage and grows without limit. The figure nonetheless stays inside a fixed circle, so a bounded region can contain a boundary of unbounded length.
overview.purpose: The student computes how the perimeter changes each stage and argues about what happens after many stages, reconciling unbounded perimeter with a bounded region.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure and circle fill the main panel with the stage slider and readouts beneath. On a 390 px frame the readouts collapse into a strip and the circle stays fully visible. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not redraw the bounding circle at any stage, and do not use a decimal perimeter to compute the next stage. A resized circle would destroy the paradox the tool is built on.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Multiplying by four thirds every stage means the perimeter after n stages is four thirds to the power n times the original, and since four thirds is greater than one this grows past any value you name. The bumps added are ever smaller, so they never push the figure outside the circle drawn at the outset. The area added each stage shrinks fast enough to total a finite amount, which is why area and perimeter behave differently. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

Each item sets the stage from its own value, shows the question, then reveals the figure, the exact perimeter and the multiplier together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The bound has to be chosen before the growth to be evidence about the growth. Breaks: Reading the circle as decoration rather than as the fixed bound the argument rests on. ML2 (Medium, Conceptual): A bound on the region says nothing about the length of its boundary. Breaks: Belief that a figure inside a bounded region must have a bounded perimeter. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): A display choice must not feed the computation, or the error compounds with the growth. Breaks: Treating a decimal reading as the value rather than as a rounded view of it. ML4 (Hard, Conceptual): Ever smaller pieces do not imply an ever smaller total when the count grows faster than the pieces shrink. Breaks: Growth by repeated multiplication assumed to level off. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): Unbounded perimeter is a fact about the boundary, not a licence to call every quantity here unbounded. Breaks: Generalising the unbounded perimeter to the area, so both are assumed to grow without limit.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the figure inside its bounding circle and asks whether a perimeter can grow forever while the figure stays inside. Beat 2 advances stages and the perimeter readout multiplies by four thirds each time while the circle never moves. Beat 3 turns to the enclosed area, which does settle, so the two questions are separated. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setStage, showPerimeter, showArea and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open at stage 0 with the outline inside its circle and no stage run, and ask the class to say out loud whether a boundary trapped inside that circle could grow forever. Commit the class answer on the prediction pad. Targets stage 0 with the bounding circle shown and the area hidden. Never advance a stage before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Advance through the stages one at a time so each stage replaces every middle third and the perimeter readout is multiplied by four thirds, and point out that the circle has not been redrawn. Point at the perimeter readout and then at the circle. Targets stage 3 with the perimeter shown as a fraction. Read the perimeter and the multiplier from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Show the enclosed area beside the perimeter and let another stage run, so the area climbs by an ever smaller amount while the perimeter keeps multiplying. Targets stage 4 with the area shown. Name which of the two settles and which does not, and read both from getState().truth.

hunts: CIRCLE WATCH: advance stage by stage and say what the figure does to the circle and what it does to the readout.
TIMES TEN: predict the stage at which the perimeter first passes ten times its start, then check it.
AREA AGAINST PERIMETER: turn the area readout on and describe how the two quantities part company.
EXACT AGAINST ROUNDED: switch to the decimal display and say what would go wrong if the next stage used it.

whatYouLearned: Each stage multiplies the perimeter by 4 over 3, so after n stages it is 4 over 3 to the power n times the start
A factor greater than one applied over and over carries the perimeter past any value you name
The figure never leaves the circle drawn at stage 0, so a bounded region can hold a boundary of unbounded length

extra: A coastline measured with a shorter and shorter ruler, giving a longer answer each time
A thread crumpled tighter and tighter inside the same small box
A path around a garden bed rebuilt with more and more zigzags in the same space
A hem folded into ever finer pleats along the same length of cloth
A wire pushed into more and more kinks without leaving the palm holding it
A road that grows more bends while staying inside the same valley
A border between two fields redrawn along every ditch and every furrow
textbook: The first few steps of the bumped outline sequence, drawn at least as far as step 2
The count of sides at step n of that sequence, asked for as a rule
The perimeter of the shape at step n, taken with the starting triangle side as one unit

observationsAndConclusions.why: Four segments a third as long replace three, so the length is scaled by four thirds each time, and repeated multiplication by a factor above one has no ceiling
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The perimeter readout is multiplied by four thirds at every single stage and never levels off
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Growth by repeated multiplication does not slow down, however small each individual addition looks

observationsAndConclusions.why: Every bump added is a third the size of the one before, so the total outward reach is limited even though the number of bumps is not
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The circle drawn at stage 0 is never redrawn and the figure never touches it
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A region can be bounded while the boundary that encloses it is unbounded, which is the whole point of the figure

observationsAndConclusions.why: The area added at each stage shrinks fast enough for the total to converge, while the length added does not
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The area readout climbs by smaller and smaller amounts and visibly settles
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Area and perimeter are different measurements and are entitled to behave differently under the same rule

media.description: A closed outline grows bumps inside a circle that was drawn round it at step 0 and is never touched again. Every step erases the middle third of every segment and puts two sides of a bump in its place, so three parts of the same length become four and the boundary is multiplied by four thirds. The strip under the figure draws that replacement to scale - a three-part bar with its middle erased against a four-part bar of the same part width, which is the multiplier rather than an assertion of it - and reports the boundary length as an exact fraction with a rounded decimal beside it, never instead of it. Two bars underneath share one unit and one origin: the circle's own edge length, which never moves, and the boundary length, which runs past it at the very first step while the figure is still visibly inside the circle. The slice added by the current step is carried in the second accent on the same bar, so a class can see the individual bumps shrinking while the amount added still climbs. Turning the area on adds a third bar in the same picture, climbing by ever smaller amounts against a drawn ceiling at eight fifths of the starting triangle, so one rule producing two opposite behaviours is watched rather than described. The step is capped at 5 for drawing and the read-out follows the rule past it, which is stated on screen.

concept.notation: The perimeter is written as an exact fraction with powers of four and three. The multiplier from one stage to the next is four thirds.
concept.statement: Each stage replaces every segment's middle third with two sides of a bump, so three segments become four while each is a third as long. The perimeter is therefore multiplied by four thirds every stage and grows without limit. The figure nonetheless stays inside a fixed circle, so a bounded region can contain a boundary of unbounded length.
misconceptions: Belief that a figure inside a bounded region must have a bounded perimeter.
Growth by repeated multiplication assumed to level off.
concept.why_it_is_true: Multiplying by four thirds every stage means the perimeter after n stages is four thirds to the power n times the original, and since four thirds is greater than one this grows past any value you name. The bumps added are ever smaller, so they never push the figure outside the circle drawn at the outset. The area added each stage shrinks fast enough to total a finite amount, which is why area and perimeter behave differently.
worked_numbers: A perimeter of 3 becomes 4 at stage 1, then 16 over 3, then 64 over 9.
After 10 stages it is four thirds to the power 10 times 3, about 53.
The area settles at eight fifths of the starting triangle's area.

extra: A coastline measured with a shorter and shorter ruler, giving a longer answer each time
A thread crumpled tighter and tighter inside the same small box

A hem folded into ever finer pleats along the same length of cloth
A wire pushed into more and more kinks without leaving the palm holding it
A road that grows more bends while staying inside the same valley
A border between two fields redrawn along every ditch and every furrow

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the replacement itself visible, because the commonest error at this grade is counting the two new sides and forgetting the erased middle third. The strip draws three equal parts with the middle one struck out beside four parts of the same part width; the multiplier is READ OFF that pair, never asserted. A class that has watched the erase does not later say the perimeter goes up by a third.

Beat 2 is the argument settled by a number rather than a sentence. The circle's own edge length (32.65 for a starting boundary of 27) sits on the same bar, from the same origin, as the boundary length - and the boundary bar is already past it at step 1, with 36 against 32.65, while the figure has visibly not moved. That single frame is what kills 'inside a circle, so at most the circumference'.

Beat 3 keeps both quantities in one picture on purpose. The area bar climbs by smaller and smaller amounts against its drawn ceiling at 8/5 while the boundary bar keeps multiplying, so the class sees that the same rule is entitled to make one quantity settle and the other not. Do not let 'grows for ever' be generalised from the boundary to the area - that is precisely the last learn checkpoint.

media.instructions_for_student: Every step does the same thing to every piece of the outline: cut it into three equal parts, rub out the middle one, and draw two new sides of that same length in the gap. Three parts become four parts of the same length, so the boundary is multiplied by four thirds. Slide the step and watch two things at once - the boundary number climbing, and the circle standing perfectly still. That grey bar is the circle's own edge length, and the boundary bar goes past it almost straight away while the figure is still completely inside the circle. Read the boundary as a fraction, not as the decimal beside it: the fraction is the value, the decimal is only a rounded view of it. Then turn the area on and see it do the opposite - it walks up to eight fifths of the first triangle and stops. In Practice, work each question out before you check it; the boundary number stays hidden with a '?' until your answer is in, and the Hint names the method without giving you the number.

topics.summary: Replacing every side with a four-part bump multiplies the sides by 4 and the perimeter by 4/3 each step, so the perimeter grows without bound while the shape stays inside a small circle. The learner counts sides and tracks the growing perimeter.

content.text: The Koch snowflake starts as an equilateral triangle with 3 sides. At each step every side is divided into 3 equal parts, a small triangle is raised on the middle part, and the middle part is dropped. This bump replaces one straight side with 4 equal segments. Because every side becomes 4, the number of sides is multiplied by 4 each step: 3, then 12, then 48, then 192, and after n steps it is 3 multiplied by 4 raised to n. It is easy to think the side count multiplies by 3 since each side is cut into thirds, but the raised bump adds two extra segments, so the true factor is 4.

content.text: The perimeter of the Koch snowflake is the number of sides times the length of each side. At each step the number of sides is multiplied by 4, and each side length becomes one third of what it was. So the perimeter is multiplied by 4 times 1/3, which is 4/3, every step. Starting from a triangle of perimeter 3, the perimeter goes 3, then 4, then 16/3 (about 5.33), then 64/9 (about 7.11), and keeps climbing. Because 4/3 is greater than 1, multiplying by it again and again makes the perimeter grow past any value, without limit. Yet the whole snowflake always stays inside a small circle, so a finite region can have a boundary of endless length.

At each step the number of sides is multiplied by 4, and each side length becomes one third of what it was. So the perimeter is multiplied by 4 times 1/3, which is 4/3, every step. Starting from a triangle of perimeter 3, the perimeter goes 3, then 4, then 16/3 (about 5.33), then 64/9 (about 7.11), and keeps climbing. Because 4/3 is greater than 1, multiplying by it again and again makes the perimeter grow past any value, without limit. Yet the whole snowflake always stays inside a small circle, so a finite region can have a boundary of endless length.

topics.publication_chunk: The Koch snowflake starts as an equilateral triangle with 3 sides. At each step every side is divided into 3 equal parts, a small triangle is raised on the middle part, and the middle part is dropped. This bump replaces one straight side with 4 equal segments. Because every side becomes 4, the number of sides is multiplied by 4 each step: 3, then 12, then 48, then 192, and after n steps it is 3 multiplied by 4 raised to n. It is easy to think the side count multiplies by 3 since each side is cut into thirds, but the raised bump adds two extra segments, so the true factor is 4. Seconds 30 to 55 pan a Fulani wedding blanket, with diamond-in-diamond patterns circled at three scales. Seconds 55 to 90 show Escher's `Smaller and Smaller` with lizards shrinking inward. Pause at 80s (after Escher) and ask `What rule links the temple, the blanket, and this print?` - second attempt-before-reveal, before the summary card. WHAT TO ASK AFTER: Ask `Is a printed bedsheet with many identical flowers a fractal? Why or why not?` to stress the rule that `copies inside copies` means each copy must itself contain smaller copies of the same pattern.

media.teaching_notes: Hold up a cylinder and turn it, asking for the outline at each position. Ask which solid could show both a circle and a rectangle. The corner view of a cube surprises most classes.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a profile that the named solid cannot produce from the named viewpoint; a sight line pointing from a different direction than its label; a solid drawn with a profile it never shows; a fourth solid crowding the figure; a profile drawn with interior detail rather than as an outline
